doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

chapter: Learning tunes and the dance-gig years
title: Memorizing tunes, lyrics and the bandstand look
summary: Learning tunes by melody, the old timers' advice to learn lyrics, Dylan, and helping each other in the rhythm section; Marino as an ear player.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: How do you memorize tunes? Because I saw a video of you with Dave Liebman and you’re playing “Lush Life” in the famous jazz club there in Delaware Water Gap.
You know this is not a question but it was an observation that the stage looked so small that Dave had to stand on the floor.
Yeah. The rhythm section only fit on the bandstand, yeah.
But I was thinking you know “Lush Life” is not an easy tune.
You obviously had no music stand or iPad in front of you.
No, a lot of times, no.
So the general question is how do you do that? How do you memorize those things?

Well you know off of the melody for sure. People will say a song title to me and I’ll go, “Oh I’m not sure” and I’ll say, “sing it.” And once they start singing the melody I connect. Now that doesn’t hook you up for the bridge necessarily you know. The old timers would tell me, “Learn the lyrics” which I never did. I wasn’t good at learning lyrics. But if you learn the lyrics you would never forget the bridge. And they had great little tips to help younger guys out. But I never listened to lyrics. So I missed – I didn’t like Bob Dylan for that reason. I hated his singing, and it took me years to get over that and to appreciate what he was about. And it was because of the bad singing. But you know the message that he was relaying you know and getting into that vibe. That’s the
other thing that the old timers used to do, ballads, you know knowing the lyrics of the song, they really get inside of it you know and, you know, emotion would flow out of them you know.

I liked it when I would watch a bandstand, and of course it would happen to me too. Sometimes the bass player would give the look to the piano player, or vice versa. You know the bridge is coming up and you give them the look.
You go, “Okay thanks for the look, what does it mean?”

Yeah. Well the look means – it could mean what’s the first chord, when is the bridge, do you know the bridge, I know the bridge. You know whoever the leader is in that moment, will give and take always on the bandstand. And that goes with when you’re soloing and you’re soloing on a tune you don’t know well, you have a good accompanist, a great piano player or guitar player, they help. They can sense that I don’t know this tune and maybe I blew a scale tone of a chord or I’m leading astray, I don’t know the melody that well so my rhythmic phrasing is not together. And they’ll help. They’ll throw in and let you use your ear and find yourself you know. And I kind of consider myself more of an ear player than, you know, a musician by rote. Or – I used my ear a lot, all through the years that I’ve played. And playing those dance gigs that I did in the early stages really helped me with that. You know? Because I didn’t know these tunes. I don’t think they expected me to know all of them but I’d always get help from the piano player. He’d give me a bass note or just give me the first chord ahead of time, a little bit ahead of time. So we were always helping each other in the rhythm section.
